items.stem: Identify the term for the following: “The variable that the researcher manipulates or changes between conditions”.
options: Independent variable
Natural experiment
Laboratory experiment
Operationalisation
items.answer: Independent variable
items.markingKey: Independent variable: the variable that the researcher manipulates or changes between conditions. [1]

items.stem: Assertion (A): Laboratory experiments can have low ecological validity. Reason (R): They take place in artificial settings and often use tasks unlike everyday behaviour. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
items.answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
items.markingKey: Both true; the artificial setting and tasks are the reason for low ecological validity. [1]

items.stem: Assertion (A): In a natural experiment participants can be randomly allocated to conditions. Reason (R): The researcher does not manipulate the IV in a natural experiment. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
items.answer: A is false, but R is true.
items.markingKey: A is false: because the IV occurs naturally, participants cannot be randomly allocated. R is true. [1]

items.stem: Ethan, a psychology student in Auckland, investigated whether listening to music while revising affects memory. 8 participants learned a list of 20 words in silence and 8 different participants learned the list while music with lyrics played. Each participant then wrote down as many words as they could recall. Table: Number of words recalled (out of 20) — Silence: 18, 19, 13, 11, 11, 15, 14, 16. Music with lyrics: 13, 11, 13, 10, 7, 12, 7, 11. What is the mean score for the music with lyrics condition, to one decimal place?

After a new timetable began in a school in Lagos, Isla compared stress scores of students before the change with those of students after the change. The school, not the researcher, had decided to change the timetable. Explain one weakness of this type of experiment for this study.
items.answer: Participants cannot be randomly allocated, so other differences between the two groups (participant variables) could explain any difference in stress.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: no random allocation/control; 1 mark: effect on validity [2]

items.stem: Isla wants to find out whether students in Colombo remember more vocabulary when tested in the same room in which they learned it. Half the students learn and are tested in the same classroom; half learn in a classroom and are tested in the library. (a) Identify the IV and the DV in this experiment. (b) Is this a laboratory, field or natural experiment? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) IV: whether students are tested in the same room as learning or a different room. DV: the number of vocabulary items correctly recalled. (b) A field experiment: the IV is manipulated by the researcher but the study takes place in the students’ normal school setting.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark IV; 1 mark operationalised DV [2] (b) 1 mark: field; 1 mark: reason (manipulated IV, natural setting) [2]

items.stem: ‘Laboratory experiments are the most useful method in psychology.’ Discuss this view.
items.answer: Arguments for: High control of extraneous variables allows cause-and-effect conclusions. Standardised procedures make replication and checking reliability possible (for example Dement and Kleitman’s use of EEG). Arguments against: Artificial settings and tasks reduce ecological validity. Demand characteristics may change behaviour. Some topics cannot be studied ethically in a laboratory, so natural experiments or self-reports are needed. Conclusion: a supported judgement weighing the evidence on both sides.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: accurate, detailed psychological knowledge (named studies/theories) used to build a two-sided argument; evaluation includes issues such as validity, reliability, generalisability, ethics or usefulness; a justified conclusion. Middle band: relevant knowledge with some evaluation, but one side or the conclusion is underdeveloped. Lower band: limited, mostly descriptive answer with little evaluation.

items.stem: After a new timetable began in a school in Bangkok, Sipho compared stress scores of students before the change with those of students after the change. The school, not the researcher, had decided to change the timetable. (a) Identify the type of experiment and explain your answer. (b) Explain one strength of this type of experiment for this study. (c) Explain one weakness of this type of experiment for this study.
items.answer: (a) A natural experiment, because the IV (the timetable) was changed by the school, not manipulated by the researcher. (b) It allows a real-life change to be studied that the researcher could not ethically or practically create, so it has high ecological validity. (c) Participants cannot be randomly allocated, so other differences between the two groups (participant variables) could explain any difference in stress.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: natural; 1 mark: reason [2] (b) 1 mark: strength; 1 mark: context [2] (c) 1 mark: no random allocation/control; 1 mark: effect on validity [2]

items.stem: Identify the term for the following: “The variable that the researcher manipulates or changes between conditions”.
options: Field experiment
Operationalisation
Natural experiment
Independent variable
items.answer: Independent variable
items.markingKey: Independent variable: the variable that the researcher manipulates or changes between conditions. [1]

items.stem: Which term is defined as the following: “An experimental design in which different participants take part in each condition”?
options: Repeated measures design
Standardisation
Independent measures design
Volunteer sample
items.answer: Independent measures design
items.markingKey: Independent measures design: an experimental design in which different participants take part in each condition. [1]

items.stem: Assertion (A): Independent measures designs need more participants than repeated measures designs. Reason (R): In an independent measures design each participant takes part in only one condition. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
items.answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
items.markingKey: Each person gives data for only one condition, so more people are needed. [1]

items.stem: Assertion (A): A volunteer sample is always representative of the target population. Reason (R): Volunteers choose to take part themselves. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
items.answer: A is false, but R is true.
items.markingKey: A is false; because volunteers self-select, the sample may be biased. R is true. [1]

items.stem: Aisha is testing whether people can solve anagrams faster in the morning or in the evening. Aisha plans to use the same 20 participants in both conditions, with different anagrams each time. Aisha recruits participants by asking people in the college library. Identify this sampling technique and explain one weakness.
items.answer: Opportunity sampling; people in a library may be more studious or better at word tasks, so the sample is biased and may not represent all students.
items.markingKey: 1 mark technique; 1 mark weakness in context [2]

items.stem: Arjun is testing whether people can solve anagrams faster in the morning or in the evening. Arjun plans to use the same 20 participants in both conditions, with different anagrams each time. (a) Name the experimental design and explain one advantage of it here. (b) Explain how Arjun could use counterbalancing in this study.
items.answer: (a) Repeated measures: the same participants do both conditions, so participant variables such as vocabulary ability are controlled. (b) Ten participants do the morning condition first and the evening condition second; the other ten do the evening condition first, so practice effects are balanced.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark design; 1 mark advantage in context [2] (b) 1 mark split into two orders; 1 mark purpose [2]

items.stem: Daniel is testing whether people can solve anagrams faster in the morning or in the evening. Daniel plans to use the same 20 participants in both conditions, with different anagrams each time. (a) Explain how Daniel could use counterbalancing in this study. (b) Daniel recruits participants by asking people in the college library. Identify this sampling technique and explain one weakness.
items.answer: (a) Ten participants do the morning condition first and the evening condition second; the other ten do the evening condition first, so practice effects are balanced. (b) Opportunity sampling; people in a library may be more studious or better at word tasks, so the sample is biased and may not represent all students.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark split into two orders; 1 mark purpose [2] (b) 1 mark technique; 1 mark weakness in context [2]

items.stem: Isla is testing whether people can solve anagrams faster in the morning or in the evening. Isla plans to use the same 20 participants in both conditions, with different anagrams each time. (a) Explain how Isla could use counterbalancing in this study. (b) Explain why the two sets of anagrams must be equally difficult.
items.answer: (a) Ten participants do the morning condition first and the evening condition second; the other ten do the evening condition first, so practice effects are balanced. (b) If one set is easier, the difficulty of the anagrams (not the time of day) could explain the difference in solving time, so it would be a confounding variable.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark split into two orders; 1 mark purpose [2] (b) 1 mark: difficulty would confound; 1 mark: cannot conclude time of day caused the effect [2]

items.stem: Jonas is testing whether people can solve anagrams faster in the morning or in the evening. Jonas plans to use the same 20 participants in both conditions, with different anagrams each time. (a) Name the experimental design and explain one advantage of it here. (b) Explain why the two sets of anagrams must be equally difficult.
items.answer: (a) Repeated measures: the same participants do both conditions, so participant variables such as vocabulary ability are controlled. (b) If one set is easier, the difficulty of the anagrams (not the time of day) could explain the difference in solving time, so it would be a confounding variable.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark design; 1 mark advantage in context [2] (b) 1 mark: difficulty would confound; 1 mark: cannot conclude time of day caused the effect [2]

items.stem: A student writes: “A matched pairs design means the same people take part in both conditions.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. That is repeated measures; in matched pairs different but similar people (matched on key variables) do each condition.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: correct judgement; 1 mark: accurate explanation [2]

items.stem: Which term is defined as the following: “A method in which participants give information about themselves, for example in a questionnaire or interview”?
options: Self-report
Social desirability bias
Case study
Open question
items.answer: Self-report
items.markingKey: Self-report: a method in which participants give information about themselves, for example in a questionnaire or interview. [1]

items.stem: Assertion (A): Case studies have low generalisability. Reason (R): Case studies usually focus on one person or a very small group. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
items.answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
items.markingKey: A unique individual may not represent others, so findings may not generalise. [1]

items.stem: Assertion (A): Covert observations avoid demand characteristics. Reason (R): In covert observations participants give informed consent. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
items.answer: A is true, but R is false.
items.markingKey: A is true; R is false: covert observations do not obtain consent, which is why participants behave naturally. [1]

items.stem: A researcher in Dhaka observes children in a school playground to study sharing behaviour. The researcher sits on a bench, unseen by the children, and records behaviour every 30 seconds. Identify two features of this observation.
items.answer: Covert (children do not know) and non-participant (the researcher does not join in); also naturalistic and using time sampling.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each feature [2]

items.stem: Ana wants to find out about the sleep habits of teenagers in Doha. Ana is deciding between a questionnaire and an interview. (a) Explain one reason why the teenagers might not answer truthfully. (b) Explain one advantage of a questionnaire over an interview for this study.
items.answer: (a) Social desirability: they may report more sleep or less phone use than is true so that they appear sensible; or they may not remember accurately. (b) A questionnaire can be given to many teenagers quickly and anonymously, so more data are collected and answers may be more honest.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark reason; 1 mark explained in context [2] (b) 1 mark advantage; 1 mark explained [2]

items.stem: A researcher in Mexico City observes children in a school playground to study sharing behaviour. The researcher sits on a bench, unseen by the children, and records behaviour every 30 seconds. (a) Explain one ethical issue in this observation and how it could be dealt with. (b) Explain why a second observer would improve the study.
items.answer: (a) Children cannot give informed consent and are not aware; consent should be obtained from the school and parents beforehand and data kept confidential. (b) Two observers recording independently allow inter-rater reliability to be checked by correlating their records.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark issue; 1 mark solution [2] (b) 1 mark: two independent records; 1 mark: inter-rater reliability [2]

items.stem: Nadia wants to find out about the sleep habits of teenagers in Mexico City. Nadia is deciding between a questionnaire and an interview. (a) Write one closed question Nadia could use. (b) Explain one reason why the teenagers might not answer truthfully. (c) Explain one advantage of a questionnaire over an interview for this study.
items.answer: (a) For example: “On a school night, how many hours do you usually sleep? Less than 6 / 6–7 / 7–8 / more than 8.” (b) Social desirability: they may report more sleep or less phone use than is true so that they appear sensible; or they may not remember accurately. (c) A questionnaire can be given to many teenagers quickly and anonymously, so more data are collected and answers may be more honest.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark closed format; 1 mark relevant to sleep habits [2] (b) 1 mark reason; 1 mark explained in context [2] (c) 1 mark advantage; 1 mark explained [2]

items.stem: Which term is defined as the following: “A relationship in which, as one co-variable increases, the other also increases”?
options: Positive correlation
Quantitative data
Standard deviation
Negative correlation
items.answer: Positive correlation
items.markingKey: Positive correlation: a relationship in which, as one co-variable increases, the other also increases. [1]

items.stem: Assertion (A): A correlation cannot show cause and effect. Reason (R): In a correlation neither co-variable is manipulated. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
items.answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
items.markingKey: Without manipulation, a third variable or reversed causation could explain the relationship. [1]

items.stem: Assertion (A): The median is the best measure of central tendency for data with an outlier. Reason (R): The median uses the value of every score in its calculation. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
items.answer: A is true, but R is false.
items.markingKey: A is true; R is false: the median is not calculated from every value, which is why it is not distorted. [1]

items.stem: Mateo tested whether a smile increases helping. Over 6 sessions with a smiling server and 6 sessions with a neutral server in a café in Manila, the number of customers out of 30 who returned their tray was recorded. Table: Trays returned (out of 30) per session — Smiling server: 17, 19, 15, 7, 14, 17. Neutral server: 11, 8, 15, 3, 9, 10. Identify the independent variable (IV) and the dependent variable (DV) in this study.
items.answer: IV: whether the server smiled or kept a neutral expression. DV: the number of customers out of 30 per session who returned their tray.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: IV; 1 mark: DV, operationalised [2]

items.stem: Yusuf tested whether a smile increases helping. Over 6 sessions with a smiling server and 6 sessions with a neutral server in a café in Manila, the number of customers out of 30 who returned their tray was recorded. Table: Trays returned (out of 30) per session — Smiling server: 17, 17, 24, 20, 19, 19. Neutral server: 12, 8, 12, 7, 13, 17. (a) Calculate the percentage of participants in the smiling server condition who scored 17 or more. Show your working. (b) Using the mean scores, state one conclusion that can be drawn from these results.
items.answer: (a) 100% (b) The smiling server condition had a higher mean (19.3) than the neutral server condition (11.5), suggesting that a smiling server encourages more helpful behaviour from customers.
items.markingKey: (a) 6 out of 6 participants scored 17 or more: 6 ÷ 6 × 100 = 100%. 1 mark working; 1 mark answer [2] (b) 1 mark: conclusion about the effect of the IV on the DV; 1 mark: supported with the means [2]

items.stem: In a field experiment in a café in Nairobi, Noah investigated whether a smiling server receives more help. On some days the server smiled at every customer and on other days kept a neutral expression; the number of customers (out of 30 per session) who returned their tray was counted. Table: Trays returned (out of 30) per session — Smiling server: 15, 12, 24, 9, 17, 15, 21, 18, 18. Neutral server: 12, 8, 30, 14, 10, 13, 12, 13, 10. (a) Identify the independent variable (IV) and the dependent variable (DV) in this study. (b) Calculate the percentage of participants in the smiling server condition who scored 14 or more. Show your working.
items.answer: (a) IV: whether the server smiled or kept a neutral expression. DV: the number of customers out of 30 per session who returned their tray. (b) 77.8%
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: IV; 1 mark: DV, operationalised [2] (b) 7 out of 9 participants scored 14 or more: 7 ÷ 9 × 100 = 77.8%. 1 mark working; 1 mark answer [2]

items.stem: ‘Quantitative data are more useful than qualitative data in psychology.’ Evaluate this statement, using evidence from psychology.
items.answer: Arguments for: Quantitative data are objective and easy to analyse and compare, for example percentages of help in Piliavin et al. They allow statistical analysis and checks of reliability. Arguments against: Qualitative data give depth and explain why people behave as they do, for example Milgram’s descriptions of tension. Numbers can oversimplify experiences such as phobias. Many studies combine both types for a fuller picture. Conclusion: a supported judgement weighing the evidence on both sides.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: accurate, detailed psychological knowledge (named studies/theories) used to build a two-sided argument; evaluation includes issues such as validity, reliability, generalisability, ethics or usefulness; a justified conclusion. Middle band: relevant knowledge with some evaluation, but one side or the conclusion is underdeveloped. Lower band: limited, mostly descriptive answer with little evaluation.

Numbers can oversimplify experiences such as phobias. Many studies combine both types for a fuller picture. Conclusion: a supported judgement weighing the evidence on both sides.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. items.stem: A student writes: “A correlation coefficient of −0.9 shows a weak relationship because the number is negative.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. The sign shows direction only; −0.9 is a strong negative correlation.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: correct judgement; 1 mark: accurate explanation [2]

items.stem: Identify the term for the following: “A prediction that there will be no difference or no relationship between the variables”.
options: Informed consent
Test–retest reliability
Null hypothesis
Generalisability
items.answer: Null hypothesis
items.markingKey: Null hypothesis: a prediction that there will be no difference or no relationship between the variables. [1]

items.stem: Assertion (A): Deception can sometimes be acceptable in psychological research. Reason (R): Some behaviour would change if participants knew the true aim. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
items.answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
items.markingKey: The BPS allows deception when it is necessary, harmless and followed by debriefing. [1]

items.stem: Assertion (A): Animal studies always generalise to humans. Reason (R): Animals and humans share some biological processes. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
items.answer: A is false, but R is true.
items.markingKey: A is false: there are important differences in brains, cognition and culture. R is true. [1]

items.stem: A researcher in Riyadh plans to study learning in rats by rewarding them with food for pressing a lever. The rats will be kept in cages in a laboratory for several weeks. Explain one reason why findings from rats may not generalise to humans.
items.answer: Human learning involves cognition, language and culture, so results from rats pressing levers may not explain complex human behaviour.
items.markingKey: 1 mark difference; 1 mark consequence [2]

items.stem: A researcher in Muscat plans to study learning in rats by rewarding them with food for pressing a lever. The rats will be kept in cages in a laboratory for several weeks. (a) Explain how the researcher could apply the principle of reduction. (b) Explain how the researcher could apply the principle of refinement.
items.answer: (a) Use the smallest number of rats needed to obtain valid results, for example by using a good experimental design and statistics. (b) Provide suitable housing with companions and enrichment, handle rats gently and avoid food deprivation that causes distress.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: fewest animals; 1 mark: how [2] (b) 1 mark: reduce suffering; 1 mark: example [2]

items.stem: A researcher in Riyadh plans to study learning in rats by rewarding them with food for pressing a lever. The rats will be kept in cages in a laboratory for several weeks. (a) Explain how the researcher could apply the principle of refinement. (b) Explain one reason why findings from rats may not generalise to humans.
items.answer: (a) Provide suitable housing with companions and enrichment, handle rats gently and avoid food deprivation that causes distress. (b) Human learning involves cognition, language and culture, so results from rats pressing levers may not explain complex human behaviour.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: reduce suffering; 1 mark: example [2] (b) 1 mark difference; 1 mark consequence [2]

items.stem: Identify the term for the following: “The variable that is measured to see whether it has been affected by the independent variable”.
options: Field experiment
Laboratory experiment
Confounding variable
Dependent variable
items.answer: Dependent variable
items.markingKey: Dependent variable: the variable that is measured to see whether it has been affected by the independent variable. [1]

items.stem: Assertion (A): Field experiments may raise ethical problems. Reason (R): Participants in field experiments often do not know they are being studied. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
items.answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
items.markingKey: Lack of consent and debriefing in natural settings causes the ethical problem. [1]

items.stem: A researcher in Kathmandu tested the effect of background music on recall. Participants were randomly allocated to learn 20 words either in silence or with song lyrics playing, then recalled the words. Table: Number of words recalled (out of 20) — Silence: 10, 14, 11, 10, 11, 15. Music with lyrics: 12, 11, 11, 8, 12, 9. Explain one ethical issue that the researcher should consider in this study.
items.answer: Right to withdraw: participants who find the recall test stressful should be told they can leave at any time.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: ethical guideline named; 1 mark: applied to this study [2]

items.stem: Nadia, a psychology student in Dubai, investigated whether listening to music while revising affects memory. 7 participants learned a list of 20 words in silence and 7 different participants learned the list while music with lyrics played. Each participant then wrote down as many words as they could recall. Table: Number of words recalled (out of 20) — Silence: 10, 9, 10, 10, 20, 11, 6. Music with lyrics: 10, 9, 8, 11, 9, 7, 7. (a) Identify the independent variable (IV) and the dependent variable (DV) in this study. (b) The participants were people who were in the college canteen at lunchtime when Nadia was collecting data. Identify the sampling technique used and explain one weakness of it.
items.answer: (a) IV: whether participants learned the words in silence or with music with lyrics playing. DV: the number of words (out of 20) correctly recalled. (b) Opportunity sampling. Weakness: only people present at that place and time could be chosen, so the sample may be biased and not representative of the target population.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: IV; 1 mark: DV, operationalised [2] (b) 1 mark: sampling technique; 1 mark: weakness explained [2]

Conclusion: a supported judgement weighing the evidence on both sides.

items.stem: Which term describes the following: “An experimental design in which the same participants take part in every condition”?
options: Opportunity sample
Volunteer sample
Repeated measures design
Counterbalancing
items.answer: Repeated measures design
items.markingKey: Repeated measures design: an experimental design in which the same participants take part in every condition. [1]

items.stem: Assertion (A): Counterbalancing removes order effects completely. Reason (R): Counterbalancing spreads order effects across both conditions. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
items.answer: A is false, but R is true.
items.markingKey: A is false: order effects still occur but are balanced out. R is true. [1]

items.stem: In a repeated measures experiment, 8 adults in Bangkok completed a computer reaction-time task after a caffeinated drink and, on another day, after an identical-tasting decaffeinated drink. Table: Reaction time (ms) — Caffeinated drink: 260, 266, 212, 285, 306, 237, 275, 263. Decaffeinated drink: 319, 252, 291, 310, 268, 330, 238, 294. The participants were people who responded to a poster in a library in Bangkok asking for participants. Identify the sampling technique used and explain one weakness of it.
items.answer: Volunteer sampling. Weakness: only people who saw the poster and chose to respond took part, so the sample may be unrepresentative.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: sampling technique; 1 mark: weakness explained [2]

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that repeated measures is the best experimental design? In your answer, you may refer to order effects and participant variables.
items.answer: Arguments for: It controls participant variables because the same people do each condition. Fewer participants are needed. Arguments against: Order effects (practice, fatigue) can affect results, although counterbalancing helps. Participants see both conditions so may guess the aim (demand characteristics). It cannot be used when the conditions involve different groups, such as males and females, or when one condition would carry over. Conclusion: a supported judgement weighing the evidence on both sides.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: accurate, detailed psychological knowledge (named studies/theories) used to build a two-sided argument; evaluation includes issues such as validity, reliability, generalisability, ethics or usefulness; a justified conclusion. Middle band: relevant knowledge with some evaluation, but one side or the conclusion is underdeveloped. Lower band: limited, mostly descriptive answer with little evaluation.

items.stem: A psychologist in Kuala Lumpur wants to compare two methods of reducing exam anxiety. 40 students with high anxiety scores are available. The psychologist is worried that some students are naturally more anxious than others. (a) Explain why a matched pairs design would be suitable. (b) Explain why a repeated measures design would not be suitable. (c) Suggest one ethical issue in this study and how it could be dealt with.
items.answer: (a) Students could be paired on their initial anxiety scores and one of each pair given each method, so differences in starting anxiety are controlled and there are no order effects. (b) Once a student has received one anxiety-reduction method its effects would carry over to the second method, so the effects could not be separated (order/carry-over effects). (c) Protection from harm: anxious students might become more distressed; they should be monitored, given the right to withdraw and offered the more effective method afterwards.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark pairing on anxiety; 1 mark benefit [2] (b) 1 mark carry-over; 1 mark consequence [2] (c) 1 mark issue; 1 mark how dealt with [2]

items.stem: Define the term ‘self-report’.
items.answer: A method in which participants give information about themselves, for example in a questionnaire or interview.
items.markingKey: Self-report: a method in which participants give information about themselves, for example in a questionnaire or interview. 1 mark for a partial definition; 2 marks for a full, accurate definition [2]

items.stem: Explain one strength and one weakness of using closed questions in a questionnaire.
items.answer: Strength: answers are quantitative, so they are quick to analyse and compare. Weakness: participants may be forced to choose an answer that does not reflect their true view, reducing validity.
items.markingKey: 1 mark strength; 1 mark weakness [2]

items.stem: Ethan carried out a structured observation of children in a playground in Cairo. Two observers watched the same children for 20 minutes and tallied behaviours. Tallies — shouting at another child: Observer 1 = 9, Observer 2 = 9; hitting another child: Observer 1 = 18, Observer 2 = 17; helping another child: Observer 1 = 16, Observer 2 = 18. Explain one ethical issue raised by this observation.
items.answer: Privacy: children should only be observed in a public place where they might expect to be seen.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: guideline; 1 mark: applied [2]

items.stem: In a revision session, a student says: “The median of 3, 8, 5, 10 is 6.5.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. In order: 3, 5, 8, 10; the median is (5 + 8) ÷ 2 = 6.5.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: correct judgement; 1 mark: accurate explanation [2]

items.stem: Assertion (A): The range is a weak measure of spread. Reason (R): The range only uses the highest and lowest scores. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
items.answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
items.markingKey: Using only two scores makes the range easily distorted by an extreme value. [1]

items.stem: Amara investigated whether the number of hours students in Madrid spend on social media each day is related to their score on a sleep-quality questionnaire (0–30, higher = better sleep). 10 students took part. Data (social-media hours, sleep-quality score) for each participant: (1, 21); (5, 17); (4, 15); (4, 14); (0, 22); (4, 16); (8, 4); (1, 22); (5, 13); (0, 24). Suggest one other variable that could explain this relationship.
items.answer: Stress about school work, which could affect both co-variables.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: plausible third variable; 1 mark: explains how it could affect both [2]

items.stem: Ethan tested whether a smile increases helping. Over 8 sessions with a smiling server and 8 sessions with a neutral server in a café in Bangkok, the number of customers out of 30 who returned their tray was recorded. Table: Trays returned (out of 30) per session — Smiling server: 18, 13, 11, 19, 15, 20, 12, 18. Neutral server: 12, 15, 16, 13, 14, 13, 10, 15. (a) Using the mean scores, state one conclusion that can be drawn from these results. (b) The standard deviation for the smiling server condition was 3.45 and for the neutral server condition was 1.93. Explain what these values show. (c) To what extent do these results support the prediction that customers served by a smiling server will return more trays than customers served by a neutral server? Use the data in your answer. (d) Suggest one improvement to this study and explain how it would improve the validity or reliability of the results.
items.answer: (a) The smiling server condition had a higher mean (15.8) than the neutral server condition (13.5), suggesting that a smiling server encourages more helpful behaviour from customers. (b) The smiling server condition has the larger standard deviation, so its scores are more spread out around the mean; the other condition’s scores are more consistent. (c) Mean for smiling server = 15.8 and neutral server = 13.5; the direction of the difference matches the prediction, but the scores in the two conditions overlap (ranges 9 and 6) and the sample is small (n = 8 per condition), so the results only partly support it; a statistical test would be needed to show the difference is significant. (d) Use a larger sample with more participants in each condition, so that anomalous individuals have less effect and the results are more reliable and generalisable.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: conclusion about the effect of the IV on the DV; 1 mark: supported with the means [2] (b) 1 mark: identifies the condition with the larger spread; 1 mark: explains that a larger SD means scores are more spread around the mean [2] (c) 1 mark: uses both means; 1 mark: judgement about direction; 1 mark: limitation such as overlap of scores, small sample or no statistical test [3] (d) 1 mark: improvement; 1 mark: how to do it; 1 mark: effect on validity/reliability explained [3]

items.stem: A student writes: “A null hypothesis predicts that the IV will have an effect on the DV.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. A null hypothesis predicts no difference or relationship.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: correct judgement; 1 mark: accurate explanation [2]

items.stem: Kwame matched 7 pairs of students in Jakarta on their previous test scores. One member of each pair revised using flash cards and the other by re-reading notes. Both then took the same 40-mark test. Table: Test score (out of 40) — Flash cards: 26, 32, 28, 36, 39, 22, 30. Re-reading: 29, 27, 28, 23, 28, 28, 21. Describe one variable that should be controlled in this study and explain why.
items.answer: The same revision time for everyone (for example 30 minutes).
items.markingKey: 1 mark: relevant control identified; 1 mark: explains how it would otherwise act as a confounding variable [2]

items.stem: Zara matched 7 pairs of students in Karachi on their previous test scores. One member of each pair revised using flash cards and the other by re-reading notes. Both then took the same 40-mark test. Table: Test score (out of 40) — Flash cards: 33, 28, 24, 30, 26, 28, 26. Re-reading: 17, 23, 22, 29, 26, 28, 23. (a) Identify the independent variable (IV) and the dependent variable (DV) in this study. (b) Name a suitable type of graph to display the mean scores for the two conditions, and justify your choice.
items.answer: (a) IV: whether students revised with flash cards or by re-reading notes. DV: score out of 40 on the same test. (b) Bar chart, because the IV has separate (discrete) categories, so the mean for each condition is shown as a separate bar with gaps between bars.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: IV; 1 mark: DV, operationalised [2] (b) 1 mark: bar chart; 1 mark: justification (discrete conditions / categories, not continuous data) [2]

items.stem: Identify the term for the following: “An experiment conducted in a controlled, artificial setting in which the researcher manipulates the IV”.
options: Field experiment
Confounding variable
Laboratory experiment
Operationalisation
items.answer: Laboratory experiment
items.markingKey: Laboratory experiment: an experiment conducted in a controlled, artificial setting in which the researcher manipulates the IV. [1]

items.stem: In a revision session, a student says: “Laboratory experiments are high in reliability because their standardised procedures can be repeated.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. Controlled, standardised procedures allow exact replication to check whether results are consistent.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: correct judgement; 1 mark: accurate explanation [2]

items.stem: A psychologist in Hanoi investigated whether being watched affects performance on a simple task. 6 participants sorted cards alone and 6 different participants sorted cards with an audience of three people. The number of cards sorted correctly in two minutes was recorded. Table: Cards sorted correctly in 2 minutes — Audience: 32, 44, 44, 39, 35, 52. Alone: 42, 37, 33, 35, 30, 39. Name the experimental design used in this study and explain one weakness of using this design here.
items.answer: Independent measures: different participants take part in each condition. Weakness: participant variables (individual differences between the two groups) may explain the difference in the DV instead of the IV.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: correct design; 1 mark: weakness explained in context [2]

items.stem: Tomás tested social facilitation: participants were randomly allocated to sort a pack of cards either alone or in front of an audience, and the number of cards sorted correctly in two minutes was counted. Table: Cards sorted correctly in 2 minutes — Audience: 27, 35, 40, 37, 30, 43, 60. Alone: 31, 35, 26, 36, 19, 35, 37. (a) Name the experimental design used in this study and explain one weakness of using this design here. (b) The standard deviation for the audience condition was 10.82 and for the alone condition was 6.60. Explain what these values show.
items.answer: (a) Independent measures: different participants take part in each condition. Weakness: participant variables (individual differences between the two groups) may explain the difference in the DV instead of the IV. (b) The audience condition has the larger standard deviation, so its scores are more spread out around the mean; the other condition’s scores are more consistent.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: correct design; 1 mark: weakness explained in context [2] (b) 1 mark: identifies the condition with the larger spread; 1 mark: explains that a larger SD means scores are more spread around the mean [2]

items.stem: Discuss whether laboratory experiments are the most useful method in psychology. In your answer, you may refer to demand characteristics and ecological validity.
items.answer: Arguments for: High control of extraneous variables allows cause-and-effect conclusions. Standardised procedures make replication and checking reliability possible (for example Dement and Kleitman’s use of EEG). Arguments against: Artificial settings and tasks reduce ecological validity. Demand characteristics may change behaviour. Some topics cannot be studied ethically in a laboratory, so natural experiments or self-reports are needed. Conclusion: a supported judgement weighing the evidence on both sides.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: accurate, detailed psychological knowledge (named studies/theories) used to build a two-sided argument; evaluation includes issues such as validity, reliability, generalisability, ethics or usefulness; a justified conclusion. Middle band: relevant knowledge with some evaluation, but one side or the conclusion is underdeveloped. Lower band: limited, mostly descriptive answer with little evaluation.

items.stem: Identify the term for the following: “An experimental design in which participants are paired on relevant variables and each member of a pair does a different condition”.
options: Matched pairs design
Repeated measures design
Random allocation
Volunteer sample
items.answer: Matched pairs design
items.markingKey: Matched pairs design: an experimental design in which participants are paired on relevant variables and each member of a pair does a different condition. [1]

items.stem: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of using an opportunity sample.
items.answer: Advantage: quick, easy and cheap because the researcher uses whoever is available. Disadvantage: the sample is likely to be biased and unrepresentative because only people in one place at one time can be chosen.
items.markingKey: 1 mark advantage; 1 mark disadvantage [2]

items.stem: Mohammed matched 8 pairs of students in Santiago on their previous test scores. One member of each pair revised using flash cards and the other by re-reading notes. Both then took the same 40-mark test. Table: Test score (out of 40) — Flash cards: 25, 28, 26, 24, 22, 24, 30, 28. Re-reading: 26, 18, 26, 23, 21, 21, 23, 18. Using the mean scores, state one conclusion that can be drawn from these results.
items.answer: The flash cards condition had a higher mean (25.9) than the re-reading condition (22.0), suggesting that revising with flash cards leads to higher test scores than re-reading.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: conclusion about the effect of the IV on the DV; 1 mark: supported with the means [2]

items.stem: Ines is testing whether people can solve anagrams faster in the morning or in the evening. Ines plans to use the same 20 participants in both conditions, with different anagrams each time. (a) Name the experimental design and explain one advantage of it here. (b) Explain how Ines could use counterbalancing in this study.
items.answer: (a) Repeated measures: the same participants do both conditions, so participant variables such as vocabulary ability are controlled. (b) Ten participants do the morning condition first and the evening condition second; the other ten do the evening condition first, so practice effects are balanced.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark design; 1 mark advantage in context [2] (b) 1 mark split into two orders; 1 mark purpose [2]

items.stem: ‘Repeated measures is the best experimental design.’ To what extent do you agree? In your answer, you may refer to participant variables, demand characteristics and order effects.
items.answer: Arguments for: It controls participant variables because the same people do each condition. Fewer participants are needed. Arguments against: Order effects (practice, fatigue) can affect results, although counterbalancing helps. Participants see both conditions so may guess the aim (demand characteristics). It cannot be used when the conditions involve different groups, such as males and females, or when one condition would carry over. Conclusion: a supported judgement weighing the evidence on both sides.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: accurate, detailed psychological knowledge (named studies/theories) used to build a two-sided argument; evaluation includes issues such as validity, reliability, generalisability, ethics or usefulness; a justified conclusion. Middle band: relevant knowledge with some evaluation, but one side or the conclusion is underdeveloped. Lower band: limited, mostly descriptive answer with little evaluation.

items.stem: Define the term ‘closed question’.
items.answer: A question with a fixed set of possible answers, giving quantitative data.
items.markingKey: Closed question: a question with a fixed set of possible answers, giving quantitative data. 1 mark for a partial definition; 2 marks for a full, accurate definition [2]

items.stem: Explain why an interviewer might choose a semi-structured interview rather than a structured interview.
items.answer: A semi-structured interview has some set questions but lets the interviewer ask follow-up questions, so richer and more detailed answers can be obtained; it is still partly comparable across participants.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: definition/feature; 1 mark: benefit [2]

items.stem: A researcher in Jakarta observes children in a school playground to study sharing behaviour. The researcher sits on a bench, unseen by the children, and records behaviour every 30 seconds. Explain why a second observer would improve the study.
items.answer: Two observers recording independently allow inter-rater reliability to be checked by correlating their records.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: two independent records; 1 mark: inter-rater reliability [2]

items.stem: A revision website states: “Qualitative data are easier to analyse than quantitative data.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Qualitative data must be interpreted or coded into themes, which is slow and can be subjective.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: correct judgement; 1 mark: accurate explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain one strength and one weakness of the mean as a measure of central tendency.
items.answer: Strength: it uses every score, so it is the most sensitive measure. Weakness: it is distorted by extreme scores (outliers).
items.markingKey: 1 mark strength; 1 mark weakness [2]

items.stem: Ines recorded revision hours and test score (out of 50) for 10 students in a college in Seoul. Data (revision hours, test score) for each participant: (1, 10); (10, 32); (6, 20); (10, 32); (9, 23); (5, 20); (12, 37); (8, 37); (9, 33); (12, 42). Write a non-directional hypothesis for this study.
items.answer: There will be a correlation between hours spent revising and test score out of 50.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: correlation (not difference) stated; 1 mark: both co-variables operationalised [2]

items.stem: A correlational study in Bogotá measured daily social-media use (hours) and sleep-quality score (0–30) for 9 students. Data (social-media hours, sleep-quality score) for each participant: (0, 24); (4, 19); (4, 16); (8, 5); (7, 7); (4, 17); (2, 16); (3, 16); (3, 16). (a) The correlation coefficient for these data is -0.93. Describe what this shows about the relationship. (b) Write a non-directional hypothesis for this study. (c) Write a directional hypothesis for this study. (d) Explain why Freya cannot conclude that social-media hours causes the change in sleep-quality score. (e) Suggest one other variable that could explain this relationship.
items.answer: (a) A strong negative correlation between daily hours spent on social media and sleep-quality score. (b) There will be a correlation between daily hours spent on social media and sleep-quality score. (c) There will be a negative correlation between daily hours spent on social media and sleep-quality score. (d) A correlation only shows that two variables are related; neither was manipulated, so the direction of cause is unknown and a third variable, such as having a part-time job, could affect both. (e) Having a part-time job, which could affect both co-variables.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: direction; 1 mark: strength [2] (b) 1 mark: correlation (not difference) stated; 1 mark: both co-variables operationalised [2] (c) 1 mark: direction; 1 mark: both co-variables operationalised [2] (d) 1 mark: no manipulation / relationship only; 1 mark: third variable or direction problem explained in context [2] (e) 1 mark: plausible third variable; 1 mark: explains how it could affect both [2]

items.stem: In a revision session, a student says: “Inter-rater reliability can be checked by correlating two observers’ scores.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. A high positive correlation between the observers’ records shows good inter-rater reliability.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: correct judgement; 1 mark: accurate explanation [2]

items.stem: A researcher in Lima plans to study learning in rats by rewarding them with food for pressing a lever. The rats will be kept in cages in a laboratory for several weeks. Explain how the researcher could apply the principle of reduction.
items.answer: Use the smallest number of rats needed to obtain valid results, for example by using a good experimental design and statistics.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: fewest animals; 1 mark: how [2]

items.stem: A researcher in Doha plans to study learning in rats by rewarding them with food for pressing a lever. The rats will be kept in cages in a laboratory for several weeks. (a) Explain how the researcher could apply the principle of reduction. (b) Explain one reason why findings from rats may not generalise to humans.
items.answer: (a) Use the smallest number of rats needed to obtain valid results, for example by using a good experimental design and statistics. (b) Human learning involves cognition, language and culture, so results from rats pressing levers may not explain complex human behaviour.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: fewest animals; 1 mark: how [2] (b) 1 mark difference; 1 mark consequence [2]
